opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real change in what we're competing on, not just a new product form.

In the chat era, the core question was basically: can the model give you a good answer in one turn? Capability was measured by knowledge, fluency, reasoning on a single question. Everyone optimized for benchmarks that looked like exams, and the gap between the top labs narrowed quite fast, because once you know the recipe of pre-training plus alignment, a lot of it becomes engineering and scale.

Agents change the unit of evaluation. It's no longer one answer, it's a whole task: maybe dozens or hundreds of steps, calling tools, reading results, recovering from mistakes, deciding when to stop. And what matters there is quite different. Long-horizon consistency matters. The ability to notice "I was wrong three steps ago" matters. Efficiency matters, because if each step is slow or expensive, the whole task becomes impractical. So a model that looks only slightly better in chat can be dramatically better as an agent, because small per-step reliability differences compound over a long trajectory.

That also changes how you train. In chat, you could get a lot from imitation: human-written data, preference data. For agents, you really need environments. The model has to act, get feedback from the world, and learn from outcomes. So reinforcement learning, and building good environments and verifiable reward signals, becomes a central competitive advantage. Whoever can build richer, more realistic environments at scale, and run RL stably on them, has a real moat that's harder to copy than a data recipe.

And I'd say it shifts the relationship with users too. Chat is a conversation partner; an agent is something you delegate to. Delegation requires trust. So beyond raw intelligence, things like controllability, predictability, cost, and being honest about uncertainty become part of the competition.

So for me, this is the phase where the question moves from "how smart does the model sound" to "how much real work can it actually finish." I think that's a much harder and more interesting race, and honestly it's still very early. Nobody has really won it yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents as a new competitive phase, but does not say that closed-source models moved toward agents before most people recognized that direction.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the shift from chat to agents is actually the real competition starting, not a continuation of the last one.

In the chat era, the product was the model, and the model was judged on how good one response was. The user asks a question, the model answers, and the interaction ends there. That is a single-turn world. Benchmarks measured it, users felt it, and the gap between companies was mostly a gap in pretraining scale and data quality.

Agents change what is being measured. Now the model has to carry a goal across many steps. It has to call tools, read what comes back, notice when it is wrong, and recover. A model can be very strong on one reply and still fall apart over thirty steps, because small errors compound. So the competition moves from "who gives the best answer" to "who stays reliable over a long horizon." That is a different capability, and it exposes different weaknesses.

I see three things becoming decisive.

The first is reinforcement learning on real tasks. Pretraining gives you knowledge, but it does not teach a model to plan, to verify, or to stop and ask. That comes from training in environments where the model actually acts and gets feedback. Building those environments well is now a core moat, maybe more than raw data.

The second is cost. An agent might burn hundreds of model calls on one task. If your model is twice as expensive per token, your agent is twice as expensive per task, and users notice that directly. This is why efficiency, both in architecture and in inference, matters more now than in the chat era. It is not a nice-to-have. It decides whether the product is usable at all.

The third is trust. When a model only talks, a mistake costs you a bad paragraph. When a model acts, a mistake can delete a file or send the wrong email. So reliability and the ability to express uncertainty become product features. The winner is not the model that is most impressive on a demo. It is the one people are willing to leave running without watching.

Honestly I think this is good for competition. In the chat phase, the leaders were mostly those with the most compute. In the agent phase there is more room for engineering taste, for good environment design, for being thoughtful about the full system. The gap can be closed by doing the harder, less glamorous work well.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes agents as a new phase of competition, but does not say that closed-source models moved toward agents before most people recognized agents as the right direction for general-purpose models.

astra-6.text:
I think the shift from chat to agents changes what it means for a model to be good. In chat, you ask a question and judge the response. With an agent, you give it a goal and judge whether it can actually complete the work.

That puts pressure on capabilities that a single conversation can hide. Can the model break a task into useful steps, choose the right tools, recognize when something has gone wrong, and recover? Can it maintain the goal over a long sequence of actions? A small error at each step can become a serious reliability problem across the whole task.

So the competition broadens. The underlying model still matters enormously, but the way it interacts with tools and its environment matters too. You need to train and evaluate the model on the consequences of its actions, not just on whether its answers sound convincing.

I also think cost becomes more consequential. An agent might make many model calls to finish one task. The relevant question becomes: how much time and money does it take to get a reliable result?

For me, that’s the defining change: users are delegating work. The models that earn that delegation will need to demonstrate consistent execution and good judgment about when to ask for help.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how agents change model competition, but does not state that closed-source models moved toward agents before most people recognized this as the right direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the shift from chat to agents changes what we expect from a general-purpose model. With chat, the user asks a question and judges the answer. With an agent, the user gives it a goal and expects it to carry out a sequence of actions. The model has to plan, use tools, recognize mistakes, and adjust as it goes.

That makes reliability much more important. A model can give an impressive answer in a single exchange, but if it makes a small mistake at each step of a long task, those mistakes accumulate. So the competition becomes about whether a model can consistently finish useful work, and whether it knows when it needs clarification or human intervention.

I also think this creates a tighter connection between model research and product design. The tools available to the model, the feedback it receives, and the way a task is structured all affect its performance. Better models enable better agents, while real agent tasks reveal weaknesses that can guide the next round of training.

So I see agents as a broader test of general-purpose models. The key question moves from ‘How well can it respond?’ to ‘How much can we trust it to accomplish?’
